newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Sun shines for start of Australian solar race.
newsitem.headline: Sun shines for start of Australian solar race.

text.p: Fifty seven space-age looking solar-powered cars and bicycles set off on Sunday in the fourth World Solar Challenge, a tough 3,010-km (1,870-mile) drive across Australia from Darwin to Adelaide.
"With the sun shining at full power, three of the 47 cars entered are estimated to average over 90 kmph (56 mph)," said event organiser Hans Tholstrup.
"In the midday sun, the leading vehicles will certainly have to slow down to avoid breaking the legal speed limits," he said. Australia's open roads have a 100 kmph (60 mph) speed limit.
This year's race has attracted 47 cars and 11 bicycles, valued at A$60 million.
The carbon-fibre, solar-panelled contraptions boast names like Dawn Treader, Sun Shark and Speed of Light.

Tholstrup said the winner should set a race record, arriving in Adelaide within four days, about the same time the average petrol-fuelled car takes to travel the route, which runs from north to south across the country.
The first solar car race in Australia in 1987 was won by General Motors' Sunraycer with an average speed of 66.92 kmph (41.58 mph).

The triennial event has attracted competitors ranging from multi-national car makers seeking to hone solar technology, such as Honda which is race favourite with a car called Dream after winning the 1993 event, to high schools and universities.

Honda, which won pole position with a top speed of 135 kmph (84 mph), led the vehicles out of Darwin on Sunday morning under a blazing sun and with the temperature already hitting 30 degrees Celsius (86 Fahrenheit).

Along the Sturt Highway between Darwin and Adelaide, which passes Australia's famous Uluru (Ayers Rock), temperatures can hit 40 degrees Celsius (104 Fahrenheit). Drivers, many bolted inside their vehicles, must carry one litre of water because of the heavy loss of body fluid through perspiration.
In second place was the Swiss car Schooler, followed by France's Helios and Japan's Aisol III in fourth.

Honda officials say the Dream, which looks like a cockroach covered with monocrystal silicon cells, can cruise at more than 90 kmph (56 mph), with a top speed of 140 kmph (87 mph). The Dream is the first two-seater car to enter the solar race.

Competitors race between 8.00 a.m. and 5.00 p.m. and must maintain a minimum speed of 40 kmph (25 mph). Each night teams camp in the outback where their vehicles stop. Race inspectors check that batteries are not recharged overnight.

Tholstrup, who created the world's first solar car in 1982, calls the event "Brain Sport" as it aims to encourage research and development for environmentally friendly and sustainable energy for the future.
In 1982, Tholstrup and a co-driver steered their BP Quiet Achiever vehicle 4,056 km (2,520 miles) from Perth on the west Australian coast to Sydney on the east coast.
